subject: Nvidia
angle: Three engineers planned Nvidia at a Denny's diner in 1993; near-bankruptcy in the 90s; the bet on graphics chips that later became the engine of AI.

subject: Airbnb
angle: Two designers rented air mattresses in their apartment in 2007, sold custom cereal boxes to survive, got rejected by investors, then Y Combinator.

subject: History of Amazon
angle: Bezos left a Wall Street job in 1994 to sell books online from a garage; the early years of losses before profit.

subject: History of Apple Inc.
angle: Jobs and Wozniak building the Apple I in 1976, selling a van and a calculator to fund it; the Apple II and the first IPO.

subject: History of Google
angle: Two Stanford PhD students, a search engine first called BackRub, the $100,000 cheque written before the company existed, the garage in Menlo Park.

subject: OpenAI
angle: Founded in 2015 as a non-profit with a pledge of $1 billion; the shift to a capped-profit model; Microsoft's investment; ChatGPT.

subject: SpaceX
angle: The first three Falcon 1 launches failed; the fourth in 2008 succeeded with money for one more try; NASA contract days later.

subject: Stripe, Inc.
angle: Two Irish teenage brothers who sold their first company, then built seven lines of code that let websites take payments; Y Combinator; valuation history.

subject: Shopify
angle: Tobias Lütke wanted to sell snowboards online in 2004, hated the software available, built his own store software, and that became the product.

subject: Slack Technologies
angle: Slack began as an internal chat tool for a video game that failed (Glitch); the team kept the tool and it became one of the fastest-growing business apps ever.

subject: Instagram
angle: Started as a check-in app called Burbn; the founders cut everything except photos, filters and likes; 25,000 users on day one; sold to Facebook for $1 billion with 13 employees.

subject: WhatsApp
angle: Jan Koum and Brian Acton were rejected for jobs at Facebook and Twitter; built WhatsApp; Facebook bought it in 2014 for about $19 billion.

subject: Zoom Communications
angle: Eric Yuan's US visa was refused eight times; he left Cisco WebEx to start Zoom in 2011; the pandemic made it a household name.

subject: Canva
angle: Melanie Perkins pitched to more than a hundred investors and was rejected; started with a school yearbook tool in Perth; Canva's rise to a multi-billion valuation.

subject: Google DeepMind
angle: Founded in London in 2010 to solve intelligence; Google bought it in 2014; AlphaGo; AlphaFold and the Nobel Prize.

subject: Tesla, Inc.
angle: Tesla was founded in 2003 by Eberhard and Tarpenning; Musk came in as an investor and chairman; the Roadster; the near-bankruptcy of 2008.

subject: Uber
angle: The idea came from failing to get a cab on a snowy night in Paris in 2008; UberCab in San Francisco; the fights with regulators; growth and losses.

subject: ByteDance
angle: Zhang Yiming started ByteDance in a Beijing apartment in 2012 with a news app; Douyin and TikTok; the most valuable startup in the world.

subject: Hugging Face
angle: Started as a chatbot app for teenagers; pivoted to open-source AI tools; became the home of open AI models.

subject: Netflix
angle: DVDs by mail in 1997, the subscription model, the pivot to streaming, and the decision to make its own shows.

subject: Zerodha
angle: Two brothers started a discount broker in 2010 with no outside money; zero brokerage on delivery trades; became India's largest broker and profitable without venture capital.

subject: Infosys
angle: Seven engineers started Infosys in 1981 with ₹10,000 borrowed from Narayana Murthy's wife; years to get a phone line; the 1993 IPO; global IT giant.

subject: Flipkart
angle: Two ex-Amazon engineers started selling books online from a Bangalore apartment in 2007; cash on delivery; Walmart bought a majority for $16 billion in 2018.

subject: Zomato
angle: Began as Foodiebay in 2008, scanning restaurant menus for colleagues at Bain; renamed Zomato; the 2021 IPO.

subject: Freshworks
angle: Started in Chennai in 2010 as Freshdesk after a bad customer service experience; first Indian SaaS company to list on Nasdaq in 2021.

subject: Dream11
angle: Started in 2008, nearly shut down, pivoted to daily fantasy sports; became India's first gaming unicorn.

subject: Blockbuster (retailer)
angle: Blockbuster turned down buying Netflix for $50 million in 2000; went bankrupt in 2010; Netflix is worth hundreds of billions.

subject: History of Apple Inc.
angle: Apple was weeks from bankruptcy in 1997; Jobs returned; Microsoft invested $150 million; the iMac, iPod and iPhone followed.

subject: Nokia
angle: The world's biggest phone maker chose Windows Phone over Android in 2011; market share collapsed; sold its phone business to Microsoft in 2013.

subject: Kodak
angle: A Kodak engineer built the first digital camera in 1975; the company sat on it to protect film; bankruptcy in 2012.

subject: Yahoo
angle: Yahoo passed on buying Google for about $1 million in 1998 and again for $5 billion in 2002; later declined; sold to Verizon for $4.8 billion.

subject: Amazon Web Services
angle: Amazon's internal infrastructure became a product in 2006; AWS now makes most of Amazon's profit and powers a large share of the internet.

subject: Instagram
angle: Facebook paid $1 billion for a 13-person company with no revenue in 2012; Instagram now brings in a huge share of Meta's revenue.

subject: CUDA
angle: Nvidia spent years and billions making graphics chips programmable for general computing while Wall Street doubted it; that bet made Nvidia the AI chip company.

subject: OpenAI
angle: Microsoft's $1 billion investment in OpenAI in 2019, then more than $10 billion; how it reshaped both companies and the AI race.

subject: WeWork
angle: Valued at $47 billion in 2019; the failed IPO; Adam Neumann's exit; bankruptcy in 2023.

subject: Theranos
angle: Elizabeth Holmes promised blood tests from a finger prick; $9 billion valuation; the tests did not work; convicted of fraud.

subject: FTX
angle: The crypto exchange went from a $32 billion valuation to bankruptcy in about a week in November 2022; Sam Bankman-Fried convicted.

subject: Quibi
angle: Raised $1.75 billion, launched in April 2020, shut down six months later.

subject: Juicero
angle: A $400 wifi juicer backed by $120 million; the packs could be squeezed by hand; shut down in 2017.

subject: Byju's
angle: India's most valuable startup at $22 billion; aggressive sales, missed accounts, lender fights; the collapse.

subject: Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank
angle: The bank of the startup world failed in about 48 hours in March 2023 after a run triggered on social media and group chats.

subject: Pets.com
angle: The sock puppet mascot, a Super Bowl ad, an IPO and a shutdown, all within about a year in 2000.

subject: AlexNet
angle: Three researchers in Toronto trained a neural network on two gaming GPUs and crushed the 2012 ImageNet contest; deep learning took over from there.

subject: Attention Is All You Need
angle: A 2017 Google paper with eight authors introduced the Transformer; every modern chatbot is built on it; most authors have since left to start companies.

subject: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov
angle: In 1997 an IBM machine beat the world chess champion; what the match did and did not prove.

subject: AlphaGo versus Lee Sedol
angle: In 2016 DeepMind's AlphaGo beat the Go world champion 4-1; move 37; Lee Sedol later retired saying AI cannot be defeated.

subject: ChatGPT
angle: Launched as a low-key research preview in November 2022; a million users in five days; 100 million in two months, the fastest ever.

subject: ELIZA
angle: A 1966 MIT program that pretended to be a therapist with simple pattern matching; people confided in it; its creator was alarmed.

subject: Dartmouth workshop
angle: The 1956 summer workshop where the term artificial intelligence was coined; the founders expected to make major progress in one summer.

subject: AI winter
angle: Twice, AI hype collapsed and funding vanished for years; what triggered the winters and what ended them.

subject: ImageNet
angle: Fei-Fei Li built a dataset of 14 million labelled images when most researchers thought data was not the problem; it enabled the deep learning breakthrough.

subject: AlphaFold
angle: DeepMind's AI solved the 50-year-old protein folding problem; predictions for 200 million proteins; a Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2024.

subject: Jack Ma
angle: Jack Ma failed his college entrance exam twice, was rejected from dozens of jobs including KFC (24 applied, 23 hired, he was the one turned down), and started Alibaba in 1999 in his Hangzhou apartment with 17 co-founders and about $60,000. Alibaba's 2014 IPO was the largest in history at the time.

subject: Spanx
angle: Sara Blakely was selling fax machines door to door, cut the feet off her pantyhose, and started Spanx in 2000 with $5,000 of savings, writing her own patent to avoid legal fees. Every hosiery mill turned her down until one owner's daughters talked him into it; she became the youngest self-made female billionaire in 2012.

subject: James Dyson
angle: James Dyson spent five years and built 5,127 prototypes of a bagless vacuum cleaner in his coach house, was rejected by every major manufacturer, and licensed it in Japan before launching his own company in the UK. Dyson went from near-bankruptcy to becoming one of Britain's richest people.

subject: Vijay Shekhar Sharma
angle: Vijay Shekhar Sharma grew up in a Hindi-medium school in Aligarh, learned English from cassette tapes and second-hand books, and once took a loan at 24 percent interest to keep One97 alive. He launched Paytm in 2010; demonetisation in 2016 turned it into India's biggest payments brand and the largest Indian IPO of its time in 2021.

subject: 86-DOS
angle: When IBM needed an operating system for its 1981 PC, Microsoft didn't have one. It bought 86-DOS, written by Tim Paterson at Seattle Computer Products, for about $75,000, renamed it MS-DOS and licensed it to IBM non-exclusively. That one deal built Microsoft's monopoly.

subject: Snapdeal
angle: Snapdeal was valued at $6.5 billion in 2016, then ran out of money, laid off most staff and was pushed by SoftBank to merge with Flipkart for under $1 billion. Founders Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal refused the deal in 2017, cut costs to the bone and rebuilt the company as Snapdeal 2.0.

subject: Y Combinator
angle: In 2005 Paul Graham, Jessica Livingston, Robert Morris and Trevor Blackwell ran a 'Summer Founders Program' as an experiment in batch-funding undergrads, handing 8 startups roughly $6,000 per founder plus dinners at Graham's place. That first batch contained Reddit and Justin.tv (later Twitch); the motto was 'Make something people want'.

subject: Atlassian
angle: Two UNSW graduates, Mike Cannon-Brookes and Scott Farquhar, started Atlassian in Sydney in 2002 on $10,000 of credit card debt with one goal: match the A$48,500 graduate salary their classmates were taking. They refused to hire salespeople and sold Jira online; the company IPO'd on Nasdaq in 2015.

subject: Palantir
angle: Palantir was built on the anti-fraud pattern-matching PayPal used to fight Russian scammers, and almost every Sand Hill Road firm passed — Sequoia's Michael Moritz reportedly doodled through the pitch. Peter Thiel funded it himself and the CIA's venture arm In-Q-Tel became an early backer; the name comes from the seeing-stones in Tolkien.

subject: Block, Inc.
angle: Jim McKelvey, a glassblower, lost a $2,000 sale on a glass faucet because he couldn't take an American Express card; he called his friend Jack Dorsey and in 2009 they built a card reader that plugged into an iPhone headphone jack. The square white dongle became a payments company serving the sellers banks ignored.

subject: Traitorous eight
angle: In 1957 eight scientists walked out on Nobel laureate William Shockley, who called them traitors; they signed ten one-dollar bills as their founding contract and got $1.38 million from Sherman Fairchild to start Fairchild Semiconductor. That walkout produced Intel, AMD, Kleiner Perkins and the entire venture capital model of Silicon Valley.

subject: Luis von Ahn
angle: Luis von Ahn invented CAPTCHA to stop bots, then realised he was wasting 500,000 human hours a day and rebuilt it as reCAPTCHA, which quietly used those keystrokes to digitise old books and the New York Times archive. He sold it to Google in 2009, won a MacArthur 'genius' grant, and used the same trick-humans-into-useful-work idea to build Duolingo.

subject: Zoho Corporation
angle: Sridhar Vembu started AdventNet in 1996 and has never taken outside investment or gone public, while competing with Salesforce and Microsoft. He moved his headquarters to rural Tenkasi in Tamil Nadu and built Zoho Schools to hire teenagers straight out of high school without college degrees.

subject: Odeo
angle: Odeo was a podcasting startup until Apple built podcasts into iTunes in 2005 and killed its entire market overnight. During a hackathon to find something else to do, Jack Dorsey and Noah Glass sketched a status-update service called twttr; Evan Williams then bought the company back from its own investors, who thought they were getting nothing.

subject: Andrew Grove
angle: In 1985 Japanese rivals were destroying Intel's memory-chip business, and Andy Grove asked Gordon Moore: if the board fired us and brought in a new CEO, what would he do? Moore said get out of memories — so Grove said, why don't we walk out the door, come back in and do it ourselves. Intel abandoned the product it was founded on and became a microprocessor company.

subject: Adobe Inc.
angle: John Warnock and Charles Geschke left Xerox PARC in 1982 because Xerox refused to commercialise their page-description technology. Steve Jobs offered to buy the young Adobe outright for about $5 million; they said no, and instead licensed PostScript to Apple for the LaserWriter, launching desktop publishing and making Apple's 19% stake enormously profitable.

subject: Azim Premji
angle: Azim Premji was a 21-year-old engineering student at Stanford when his father died in 1966 and he flew home to run a vegetable oil company; a shareholder told him at his first meeting to sell out because a boy couldn't run it. When IBM was forced out of India in the late 1970s, he pushed the cooking-oil firm into computers, and later gave away tens of billions to philanthropy.

subject: Wirecard
angle: Wirecard was Germany's fintech champion, in the DAX index and worth more than Deutsche Bank, until auditors admitted in June 2020 that €1.9 billion sitting in Philippine trust accounts simply did not exist. The Financial Times had reported the fraud for years while the regulator BaFin banned short selling and investigated the journalists instead; COO Jan Marsalek vanished and is still a fugitive.

subject: Nikola Corporation
angle: Nikola briefly had a market value larger than Ford without selling a single truck, until a short-seller report showed its flagship 'in motion' promo video was a prototype rolled down a hill with no working powertrain. Founder Trevor Milton was convicted of fraud in 2022 and sentenced to prison.

subject: Satyam scandal
angle: In January 2009 Satyam's chairman B. Ramalinga Raju sent a confession letter admitting he had inflated the company's cash balance by over ₹5,000 crore and that it was 'like riding a tiger, not knowing how to get off without being eaten'. India's fourth-largest IT firm collapsed days after winning a global governance award, and Tech Mahindra bought the wreckage.

subject: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
angle: Alan Turing opened his 1950 paper by calling 'Can machines think?' a meaningless question and replacing it with the imitation game. He predicted that by 2000 a machine with about a gigabyte of memory would fool interrogators 30% of the time in five minutes, and answered nine objections in advance — including Ada Lovelace's claim that machines can only do what we tell them.

subject: Tay (chatbot)
angle: Microsoft launched Tay on Twitter in March 2016 as a teenage chatbot that learned from conversation, and trolls coordinated to feed it hate speech. Within 16 hours it had posted about 96,000 tweets and Microsoft pulled it — the first mass-audience lesson that a model becomes whatever its input data is.
